Article Title: Microsoft's top AI boss has a message for engineers using GitHub Copilot: Your token spend is now being tracked
Article Text:
The company that sells AI is now rationing it internally

Nadella called himself a tokenmaxxer two months before the memo landed

Amazon, Adobe, Citi and Meta got here first

Microsoft has spent three years telling the world to use more AI. This week it told its own engineers to use it more carefully. In an internal email to his CoreAI organisation, executive vice president Jay Parikh wrote that "tokenmaxxing is not what we are optimizing for" — and backed the line with policy. OpenAI's cheaper GPT-5.6 is now the default model for internal use, every Microsoft division has an AI token budget target, and employees can pull up a dashboard showing exactly what their own AI habit costs the company.The memo was first reported by 404 Media, which obtained it from a Microsoft employee who asked not to be named. The numbers inside are the eye-catching part. Microsoft's internal Copilot guidelines say many engineers spend anywhere from a few hundred dollars to a few thousand dollars a month on tokens. No hard cap figure has been shared yet, but the guidelines warn that further restrictions may follow as spending is monitored.Parikh framed the change as discipline, not distress. "As we accelerate our use of GitHub Copilot to deliver on our goals, we all need to be aware of how we consume tokens," he wrote, adding that Microsoft would manage token spend with the same discipline it applies to every other critical resource.He was careful to say this is not a retreat from being AI-first. "We are not optimizing for fewer tokens. We are optimizing for more impact per token. "The financial context supports him. Microsoft's latest earnings beat Wall Street on revenue, operating income and net income. This is not a company scrambling for cash. It is a company discovering that agentic coding tools consume tokens at a rate nobody budgeted for. Per-token prices have dropped roughly 98 percent since late 2022, yet enterprise AI bills have tripled, because an autonomous agent chewing through a repository burns through vastly more than an autocomplete suggestion ever did.The shift did not come out of nowhere. In June, at a live taping of the New York Times' Hard Fork podcast, Satya Nadella was asked how much tokenmaxxing happens inside Microsoft. "A lot," he said, cutting off the question. "I'm a tokenmaxxer too, it's addictive. But you have to step back when the novelty wears off to say, 'What is it that I'm trying to create?'" His advice then was to match the model to the task. Don't use frontier models for non-frontier problems.Microsoft had already been trimming. It cancelled most Claude Code licences in its Experiences and Devices group in May, pushing engineers to GitHub Copilot CLI before the fiscal year closed on June 30.Microsoft is arguably the last big name to formalise this. Amazon, Adobe, Atlassian and Citi have all introduced some form of AI throttling or spend visibility. Meta shut down "Claudeonomics," an internal leaderboard that had employees competing to burn tokens.Not everyone inside Redmond reads it as prudence. The employee who leaked the memo called it "the ultimate admission" that a company hosting AI infrastructure cannot afford its own AI products, and asked the obvious follow-up: how could the companies Microsoft sells to manage?Parikh's answer is in the memo itself. Keep using AI. Just know the bill has a name on it now, and it might be yours.
Article Summary: Microsoft has spent three years telling the world to use more AI. This week it told its own engineers to use it more carefully. In an internal email to his CoreAI organisation, executive vice president Jay Parikh wrote that "tokenmaxxing is not what we are optimizing for"

Article Title: Two solar farms in Minnesota restored wildflowers, grasses and have population of bees, butterflies, wasps; scientists call it evidence of…
Article Text:
Two solar farms in Minnesota restored wildflowers, grasses and have population of bees, butterflies, wasps

The insect count that turned a Minnesota solar site into a research case study

Panel height quietly decides how much wildlife a solar farm can support

Native prairie habitat costs less than gravel across a solar farm's 25-year life

Most American solar farms still have no pollinator habitat at all

Two solar farms in Minnesota were built on retired agricultural land, and instead of the gravel or mown turf that usually goes under panels, the ground was seeded with native wildflowers and prairie grasses. Researchers from Argonne National Laboratory came back to the same test plots for five years and counted what flew and crawled past them. Insect abundance tripled. Native bees went up twentyfold.Bees, butterflies, wasps and hornets all turned up in greater numbers as the plantings matured. Lee Walston, the landscape ecologist who ran the fieldwork, builds his research around a plain question: "If you build it, will they come?" On land that used to grow row crops, the answer is yes—provided the right plants go into the soil.At an 18-acre site in Ramsey, north of Minneapolis, the method is unglamorous. Plastic flags mark the tracts, students walk the rows with clipboards, and everything spotted gets logged—a metallic green sweat bee here, a moth and two hoverflies there. Acoustic monitoring at the same site has picked up 73 bird species, drawn by the seeds and the insects. Some of them nest in the steel supports holding up the panels. The timing gives the numbers weight.Monarch butterflies are under federal review for endangered listing, and North American bird populations have fallen almost 30 percent since 1970.The Ramsey meadow exists because the panels sit higher than standard. A prairie restoration firm told ENGIE, the developer, that raising the arrays would let far more native species grow underneath without shading the glass. The extra steel and seed barely moved the project budget, and the site now needs a fraction of the mowing it otherwise would. Lower arrays leave landscapers with clover and a few grasses—better than gravel, nowhere near a prairie.The economics are less charming than the butterflies but more persuasive. Costed across 25 years, a native grass-and-forb mix works out to roughly $14,150 an acre, against $16,800 for standard turf grass and $25,000 for gravel. Maintenance drops sharply once the natives establish, usually after three or four years. There is a return at the farm gate too. A Nature Conservancy study in New Jersey found squash and blueberry yields rose 80 percent near pollinator habitat, with tomatoes, peppers, cucumbers and apples gaining 10 to 20 percent.Scale is where the story deflates. About 24,000 acres of US solar carry documented pollinator habitat, against roughly 600,000 acres of operating utility-scale sites, and meeting national energy targets could take close to 10 million acres of panels. At least 15 states run pollinator scorecards, but they largely rely on developer promises with no monitoring attached. One California project marketed as a pollinator solar farm pledged more than 200 native trees and shrubs along its perimeter; a UC Davis ecologist who walked the fence line found invasive grasses, yellow star thistle and the remains of a few plantings. The Xerces Society and an industry-funded research group are drafting a certification that would require 15 percent of a site's vegetated area to carry a diverse native mix.The Minnesota plots have settled the ecological question. What they cannot settle is whether the rest of the industry will pay for the taller steel.
Article Summary: Two solar farms in Minnesota restored wildflowers, grasses and have population of bees, butterflies, wasps and hornets. Most American solar farms still have no pollinator habitat at all. Costed across 25 years, a native grass-and-forb mix works out to roughly $14,150.

Article Title: SK Hynix commits $38 billion to two new chip fabs as AI memory demand refuses to cool
Article Text:
Image: SK Hynix

Yongin gets DRAM and HBM, Cheongju gets NAND

Memory prices are unlikely to soften before 2029

SK Hynix will spend 54 trillion Korean won, roughly $38.1 billion, on two new memory chip plants in South Korea, a bet that the AI data centre buildout still has years of runway left. The company's board approved the plan on Friday, splitting the money between a fabrication plant in Yongin, south of Seoul, and a second facility in Cheongju in the centre of the country.Neither one will produce a chip this decade's midpoint. The Cheongju fab breaks ground in February 2027 and opens its first cleanroom in December 2028. Yongin starts construction in July 2027, with its first cleanroom running by June 2029. So for anyone hoping this eases the memory crunch pushing up prices on phones, consoles and PCs, the answer is no, not for a while.The larger share, 35.2 trillion won, goes to the Yongin plant, internally called Y2. It will make DRAM, including the high-bandwidth memory that Nvidia's accelerators consume in enormous quantity. Y2 is the second of four fabs planned for the Yongin Semiconductor Cluster. The remaining 19.1 trillion won funds M17 in Cheongju, which will build NAND flash, a product SK Hynix says is seeing demand surge rapidly.Both sit inside a much bigger commitment announced last year: 600 trillion won for Yongin and 100 trillion won for Cheongju over time. SK Hynix pointed to Omdia forecasts showing DRAM and NAND demand growing 19% a year through 2030, and said the decision followed a thorough review of market demand.The timing matters because SK Hynix is under pressure at home. Samsung retook the top spot in DRAM market share during the second quarter, according to Counterpoint Research. "This has prompted SK Hynix to inject fresh capex to expand its footprint," Counterpoint's Neil Shah told CNBC, adding that it is built for 2029 and beyond rather than the current cycle.Shah expects supply from Samsung, SK Hynix, Micron and CXMT to expand significantly through 2028, but with demand outrunning planned capacity, he does not see prices easing before the end of that year. Micron has already walked away from consumer memory entirely to chase AI margins.
Article Summary: SK Hynix will spend 54 trillion Korean won, roughly $38.1 billion, on two new memory chip plants in South Korea. The company's board approved the plan on Friday, splitting the money between a fabrication plant in Yongin, south of Seoul, and a second facility in Cheongju.

Article Title: One of the world's popular jeans makers hacked: Read company’s full statement
Article Text:
Representative image

‘Corporate data extracted, operations unaffected’

Levi Strauss & Co. (the “Company”) recently detected that the Company experienced a cybersecurity incident in which an unauthorized third party gained access to Company files through social engineering techniques that enabled unauthorized access to three employees’ Company-issued computers. Following such detection, the Company initiated response protocols, implemented containment measures, launched an investigation, which remains ongoing and engaged the services of third-party cybersecurity experts.

Based on preliminary findings from the Company’s investigation, the Company believes that certain corporate information was accessed and exfiltrated as a result of the incident. As of the date of this filing, the Company believes that its rapid response efforts successfully contained and terminated the unauthorized access, and that no consumer data was impacted. The Company has not experienced any interruption in business operations as a result of the incident.

Based on information available as of the date of this filing, the Company does not believe the incident has had, or is reasonably likely to have, a material impact on the Company’s business strategy, operations, financial condition, or results of operations.

The Company has provided and will provide notifications to affected parties and applicable regulators as appropriate and in accordance with applicable law.

Part of a broader phone-based cyber campaign

Levi Strauss has disclosed that it fell victim to a recent cybersecurity incident after hackers gained access to its corporate network through a targeted social engineering attack on company personnel. The iconic jeans maker revealed the breach in a regulatory filing, stating that an unauthorised third party managed to breach its systems by tricking three employees into handing over access credentials.News agency Reuters reports that Levi Strauss joins a growing wave of global corporations facing aggressive cyber campaigns that aim to steal proprietary data and disrupt business operations.Following the intrusion, Levi Strauss initiated containment protocols and launched an internal investigation to determine the scope of the exposure, the company said. Preliminary findings indicate that attackers managed to view and extract certain internal corporate information. However, the company confirmed that its retail stores, e-commerce platforms, and daily supply chain operations experienced no disruptions.Executive leadership noted in the filing that the incident is not expected to have a material impact on the company's financial performance or operational strategy.The breach at Levi Strauss appears to be part of a larger, coordinated cyber campaign targeting major corporations across the US. Analysis of internet intelligence data reveals that ransom-seeking cybercriminals have increasingly relied on voice phishing, using phone calls to impersonate IT support or authority figures, to compromise corporate networks. Over the past five weeks alone, hackers created digital infrastructure traps targeting more than 200 companies, including prominent financial institutions and major brands.
Article Summary: The jeans maker revealed the breach in a regulatory filing. An unauthorised third party managed to breach its systems by tricking three employees into handing over access credentials. Levi Strauss joins a growing wave of global corporations facing aggressive cyber campaigns that aim to steal proprietary data and disrupt business operations.

Article Title: In 1962, a Wisconsin entrepreneur turned bus radio dispatch technology into America's first mobile pizza kitchen
Article Text:
Representative Image

How bus dispatch technology inspired mobile pizza kitchens

How pizza delivery changed in the US after World War II

Technical challenges limited the idea

"It'd be like Cirque du Soleil, basically,"

"Convenience is great, I get it,"

Expansion and eventual closure

Pizza once came from moving kitchens in America. In 1962, Wisconsin entrepreneur Dennis J. Sheahan adapted the radio dispatch technology he had developed for buses to launch Pizza on Wheels, a service that baked pizzas in specially equipped trucks while they drove to customers' homes. The idea turned bus communication systems into what became America's first mobile pizza kitchens.Customers placed orders through a central dispatcher, who used two-way radio to contact the nearest available truck. While the vehicle travelled to the delivery address, a chef inside prepared and baked the pizza so it could be served immediately after arrival. More than five decades before startups experimented with cooking pizzas in moving vehicles, Sheahan had already attempted the concept using mid-20th century technology.Sheahan, based in Reedsville, Wisconsin, had built radio dispatch systems for bus operators during the late 1950s. He later applied the same communication network to food delivery.Each Pizza on Wheels van was fitted with water tanks, sinks, refrigeration units, preparation counters and double-deck ovens. Customers called a central phone number, where a dispatcher received the order and then used radio equipment to identify the closest truck.Drivers then headed to the address while pizzas were assembled and baked inside the vehicle.The company advertised more than 25 topping combinations and promoted the service as delivering pizzas directly from the oven to customers' driveways.Pizza delivery in the US expanded rapidly after World War II as returning soldiers helped popularise the dish, while growing suburban communities and wider telephone use increased demand for home delivery.Although some pizzerias had begun offering delivery in the 1950s, orders often arrived after cooling in transit. Sheahan's mobile kitchen concept sought to solve that problem by preparing food en route rather than before delivery began.Pizza historian Carol Helstosky of the University of Denver told Popular Science that pizza has historically been suited to mobile selling, noting that pizza makers in Naples transported insulated boxes through the streets centuries before modern delivery services emerged.Despite its novelty, the concept presented practical difficulties. Refrigeration, food preparation, and oven operation inside moving vehicles posed challenges that pizza industry experts say would have been difficult to address with the technology available in the early 1960s."I've worked in the restaurant business my whole life and been a professional pizza consultant for about 15 years," Noel Brohner of Slow Rise Pizza told Popular Science. "I feel like I've heard it all." But, he admits, he'd never heard of this.Brohner also questioned how refrigeration, storage and food preparation could be managed safely inside a moving truck.Brohner said.Scott Wiener, founder of Scott's Pizza Tours, also said movement inside the vehicle would make preparing and baking pizzas considerably more difficult.Wiener stressed. "But you'll never get a quality pizza with this system."Despite the operational challenges, Pizza on Wheels expanded beyond its initial launch. After beginning with one truck in Kenosha in 1962, the company added three more vehicles in Madison the following year before expanding into Green Bay by 1964.Local newspaper advertisements from the mid-1960s also showed the company offering promotional deals and seeking franchise operators as it attempted to grow across the Midwest.By 1967, however, advertisements began appearing to sell Pizza on Wheels trucks. Some notices cited illness affecting a local operator, although the business gradually disappeared by the end of 1971.After more than 50 years had passed, the California-based company Zume tried its hand at this idea but abandoned this approach to pizza preparation in favour of other technologies before shutting down in 2023. This made “Pizza on Wheels” one of the earliest examples of such mobile-kitchen experimentation in American pizza delivery history.
Article Summary: Wisconsin entrepreneur Dennis J. Sheahan launched Pizza on Wheels in 1962. The idea turned bus communication systems into what became America's first mobile pizza kitchens. Customers placed orders through a central dispatcher, who used two-way radio to contact the nearest available truck. While the vehicle travelled to the delivery address, a chef inside prepared and baked the pizza so it could be served immediately.

Article Title: Spotify launches Premium Rewards in India, adds brand offers and invite-only events for subscribers
Article Text:
What's on offer



How subscribers can access it



Spotify has rolled out Premium Rewards in India, a new limited-edition initiative that gives Premium subscribers access to curated brand offers and invite-only live experiences, the company announced on Wednesday. The move adds a lifestyle and events layer on top of the music streaming service's existing offering of high-quality, ad-free, offline listening.Premium Rewards is built around two categories of benefits. The first is lifestyle perks — exclusive offers from partner brands including MakeMyTrip, Tira, Nykaa, Ajio Luxe, Gully Labs and Airbnb, spanning travel, beauty, fashion and lifestyle categories. The second is what Spotify is calling "IRL experiences": invite-only events, intimate listening sessions and cultural moments designed to give subscribers closer access to artists and music.Spotify says the rewards are curated around how subscribers actually live, travel and shop, positioning the initiative less as a set of discount coupons and more as an extension of the value of being a Premium member.Premium Rewards is available through a dedicated microsite, premiumrewards.byspotify.com, where Premium subscribers can browse available rewards and claim offers directly. Spotify says new perks and experiences will be added to the platform on an ongoing basis, suggesting the current lineup of brand partners and events is a starting point rather than a fixed list.The rewards program is live now and available to all Spotify Premium subscribers in India, with no separate sign-up or additional cost beyond an active Premium subscription.Shipra Srivastava, Head of Marketing at Spotify India, framed the launch as an attempt to extend Premium's value beyond the app itself. She said Premium has always centered on delivering the best audio experience — high quality, uninterrupted listening with offline access — and that Premium Rewards is meant to carry that same feeling into subscribers' everyday lives, the brands they engage with and the experiences they remember. She described the goal as making Premium function more like a membership than a plain subscription, adding that the rewards are being offered as a limited-edition experience for now, making the present moment a particularly good time to be a Premium subscriber in India.
Article Summary: Spotify has rolled out Premium Rewards in India. The initiative gives Premium subscribers access to curated brand offers and invite-only live experiences. The rewards are curated around how subscribers actually live, travel and shop. The move adds a lifestyle and events layer on top of the music streaming service's existing offering of ad-free, offline listening.

Article Title: Michael Dell's son Zach Dell aims to install a Base Power home battery system in every backyard in America; and follows what is called Costco model
Article Text:
"We want to bring Base to every neighbourhood in America over time."

Zach Dell's Base Power to replace high upfront battery costs with a membership model

“Our business model, which is very unique, is that we're really an infrastructure company. We own and operate the assets in the wholesale power markets. That's really where we make our money, not by trying to sell the consumer something at a really high-margin upfront cost,”

Customer base and manufacturing expansion

Batteries designed for homes and the power grid

"This battery is designed to be a grid resource. It's bigger, it installs faster, it switches over cleaner, it's more powerful, it has more duration,”

Michael Dell's son is expanding its battery business. Zach Dell, the co-founder of the home battery company Base Power, says he wants to install a battery system in neighbourhoods across the US. In an interview with Fortune, he said:The company follows what Dell describes as a Costco model, offering low upfront installation costs and a monthly membership instead of selling high-priced battery systems.The expansion comes as Base Power announced a $1 billion Series D funding round, valuing the company at $13 billion, up from $4 billion in less than a year. Alongside its US expansion plans, Zach Dell said the company also has ambitions to enter markets including the UK, Germany and Australia, with its business model centred on low upfront installation costs and monthly membership fees rather than large one-time equipment purchases.Founded in 2023, Base provides electricity services alongside home battery systems that act as backup power during outages. Instead of selling customers a battery system costing around $15,000 or more, the company charges an installation fee of up to $695 and a monthly membership fee of $19.Dell described the approach as similar to the Costco model, in which recurring memberships, rather than high product margins, support the business.Dell said.According to the company, the batteries also return electricity to the grid when demand is high, which it says can help lower customers' overall electricity costs.Base said it has grown from installing one battery system per day to more than 100 daily, serving over 30,000 customers. Earlier this year, the company opened its first battery manufacturing facility, Base Factory 1, in Austin, while a second, larger factory is expected to be completed in 2027.The company initially launched in Texas and has since expanded into Illinois. Dell said Base plans to enter additional US states next year by either operating in deregulated electricity markets or partnering with monopoly utilities.The Series D funding round was co-led by Ribbit Capital, Addition, Valor Equity Partners and JPMorgan Chase's Strategic Investment Group. Existing investors, including Thrive Capital, Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), Lightspeed, Trust Ventures, and CapitalG, also participated.Before opening its own manufacturing facility, Base relied on third-party battery systems. The company now produces batteries designed specifically for residential backup power and grid support rather than electric vehicle charging.Dell said.Base currently offers one- and two-battery systems. According to Dell, the company's latest battery stores 39.2 kilowatt-hours of electricity, allowing homes to continue receiving power during outages that last up to two or three days, depending on usage. Dell said the batteries are charged when electricity prices are low and supply power back to the grid when demand and prices increase.To support expansion in Illinois, Base has also introduced promotional installation pricing for some customers, reducing the installation charge from the standard $695 to as low as $95 in selected cases. Dell said the company expects to continue adjusting pricing as it enters additional markets.
Article Summary: Zach Dell's Base Power to replace high upfront battery costs with a membership model. Base Power announced a $1 billion Series D funding round, valuing the company at $13 billion. Alongside its US expansion plans, the company also has ambitions to enter markets including the UK, Germany and Australia.

Article Title: In September 2025, Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman outlined a clear red line for AI, said: AI must be shut down immediately if it ever gains …
Article Text:
Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman

‘AI’s four fatal capabilities’

“So those are the four criteria: Recursive self-improvement, setting its own goals, acquiring its own resources, and acting autonomously,

Nuclear-style regulation is not optional

Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman has outlined a firm “red line” for artificial intelligence (AI) safety, warning that if any AI system displays four specific autonomous capabilities simultaneously, it must be shut down immediately to prevent catastrophic risks. Suleyman cautioned that an AI model operating with these unrestricted capabilities could become so powerful over the next five to ten years that stopping it would require military-grade intervention.In a podcast with Trevor Noah , South African comedian and writer, in September last year, the tech executive said that to prevent such scenarios advanced frontier models must be subjected to strict auditing and oversight similar to the regulations governing critical national infrastructure like nuclear power.According to Suleyman, an AI system crosses a dangerous threshold when it combines four distinct autonomous traits. The first is recursive self-improvement, which is the ability for an AI model to rewrite, modify and optimise its own underlying source code without human input.The second is autonomous goal-setting wherein a system establishes its own objectives independent of programmer instructions. Next is the ability of autonomous action to execute decisions and interact with digital or physical systems without human authorisation.The fourth and final is the capability to independently acquire financial, computational or material resources to support its own operations.Suleyman emphasised that while individual capabilities are being researched across the industry, allowing all four to converge in a single system creates an unmanageable security threat.” Microsoft AI CEO said.Comparing the risks to high-consequence industries, Suleyman argued that developing superintelligent AI cannot remain an unregulated private enterprise.“Just like you can’t just go off and say, ‘I've got a billion dollars. I’m going to go build a nuclear power plant'... it’s a restricted activity because of the one-to-many impact it can have,” Suleyman said, urging industry leaders and governments to embrace formal regulatory frameworks.He added that tech companies and governments must collaborate on strict capability auditing before advanced models are deployed.
Article Summary: Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman has outlined a firm ‘red line’ for artificial intelligence (AI) safety. He warned that if any AI system displays four specific autonomous capabilities simultaneously, it must be shut down immediately. Sulyman cautioned that an AI model operating with these unrestricted capabilities could become so powerful over the next five to ten years that stopping it would require military-grade intervention.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Melinda Gates: When a woman can step into her full power, it’s better for her, her children, her household, her community, and her country
Article Text:
Melinda French Gates

What Melinda French Gates said about empowering women

Why Melinda Gates ' quote matters

Melinda French Gates has spent decades speaking about the importance of giving women greater opportunities and economic power. Her words on women reaching their full potential offer today’s quote of the day: “When a woman can step into her full power, it’s better for her, her children, her household, her community, and her country. ” French Gates made the remark while speaking to more than 400 people at the Denver Center for the Performing Arts on April 22. She was being honoured by the University of Denver’s Josef Korbel School of Global and Public Affairs for her work in global health, gender equity and women’s economic empowerment.The quote reflects a central idea behind much of French Gates’ philanthropic work — that helping women gain access to opportunities, resources and decision-making power can have an impact that extends beyond the individual.French Gates has been involved in philanthropy for more than 25 years. She previously co-chaired the Gates Foundation before leaving the organisation in 2024. She also founded Pivotal in 2015, an organisation focused on advancing women and young people.During her conversation with Josef Korbel School dean Frederick “Fritz” Mayer, French Gates spoke about lessons she learned from her years in philanthropy. She explained that programmes intended to solve major problems may fail to achieve their full impact when women are not considered.She pointed to drought-resistant seeds in Africa as an example. Such seeds could help farmers deal with difficult climate conditions, but their impact would be limited if women farmers could not access the merchants selling them.“[I learned that] if we didn’t focus on gender, we were basically missing half the equation,” French Gates said.The quote highlights how empowering women can create wider economic and social benefits. French Gates' argument is that when a woman has the resources and opportunities to reach her potential, the benefits can extend to her children, family, local community and eventually the wider country.Her work through Pivotal follows a similar approach. The organisation invests in underrepresented entrepreneurs and supports efforts around issues including paid family leave and increasing women's participation in public office.French Gates also stressed that making a difference does not always require large amounts of money. People can contribute their skills, knowledge and time to causes in their communities.“There are many issues in your own community that can use your services, whether that’s your intellect, your time, the way you do finances, or marketing,” she said.She added, “One person does make a difference in the life of someone else; it doesn’t always have to be big.”
Article Summary: Melinda French Gates made the remark while speaking to more than 400 people at the Denver Center for the Performing Arts on April 22. She was being honoured for her work in global health, gender equity and women’s economic empowerment. French Gates has been involved in philanthropy for more than 25 years.

Article Title: Samsung devices not just top in AI experience, but also provide advantage of ecosystem, OS upgrades and privacy
Article Text:
JB Park highlighted Samsung’s ecosystem as a defining advantage

Samsung is tailoring Galaxy AI to local needs: Jay Kim

India-specific partnerships

As AI features across smartphones increasingly start to look alike, Samsung is betting that its edge over the next few years won't come from AI alone, but from how deeply that intelligence is woven into its broader hardware, software and device ecosystem. That was the central message from JB Park, CEO and President of Samsung Southwest Asia, and Jay Kim, Corporate EVP and Head of the Customer Experience Office at Samsung's MX Division, in a roundtable discussion on the company's AI strategy.Asked what Samsung sees as its defining competitive advantage as AI capabilities converge across the industry, Park pointed to the way AI performs differently depending on the device it runs on. He noted that creative professionals often prefer editing photos and videos on the Galaxy Fold's larger foldable display over a standard bar-type phone, suggesting that AI features gain real value when paired with the right form factor.Beyond hardware, Park argued that Samsung's real strength lies in its ecosystem, which stretches well past phones and watches into home appliances and displays, all linked together so a smartphone becomes the control centre for a connected home.He pointed to AI-driven energy efficiency monitoring for appliances as one example of that connected approach. Park also flagged Samsung's commitment to seven years of OS upgrades and its focus on privacy as factors that set the company apart from rivals, framing these together as the combination that differentiates Samsung from the competition.“I think Samsung is very good in terms of ecosystem. We’re not limited to just phones and watches, but the Samsung ecosystem extends to home appliances and displays that are all linked together. You are at the centre, controlling your home appliances through a smartphone. And, you can monitor as well as make the best in terms of the energy efficiency (for appliances by using AI). We’re giving 7 years of OS upgrades and are focussed on privacy. All these factors differentiate us from competition,” Park told The Times of India.Jay Kim traced Samsung's AI evolution across recent flagship generations. The Galaxy S24, the company's first AI phone, introduced AI features tied to specific services and apps. The Galaxy S25 followed with agentic AI capabilities, including Gemini integration. With the Galaxy S26, Samsung introduced what it describes as the industry's first AI operating system, developed in collaboration with Google, representing a further step in agentic AI where the system can interpret context, automate tasks and proactively surface recommendations before users ask for them.“We're getting a lot of feedback from local markets and we will gradually apply the learnings. But I would say that we're in an early stage in terms of understanding how AI actually helps consumers’ lives every day,” said Kim.Park added that in India, Samsung has partnered with IITs and startups to improve AI usability and consumer journeys. He noted that AI usage in India is higher than the global average, with Galaxy AI features such as Photo Assist, Creative Studio, and Audio Eraser being used nearly twice as often. “In India, the usage of AI by consumers is higher than global average. Galaxy AI features such as Photo Assist, Creative Studio and Audio Eraser are used nearly twice as often as the global average. This is just the beginning of our journey for developing AI use cases in India,” added Park.
Article Summary: JB Park, CEO and President of Samsung Southwest Asia, and Jay Kim, Corporate EVP and Head of the Customer Experience Office at Samsung's MX Division, spoke at a roundtable discussion on the company's AI strategy. Park highlighted Samsung’s ecosystem as a defining advantage.

Article Title: Hollywood’s story can have a happy ending only when ..., says Paramount CEO David Ellison in open letter on Warner Bros deal

Paramount CEO David Ellison vision for Hollywood revival

Paramount Skydance reported mixed earnings results

Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison has defended the company’s proposed merger with Warner Bros. Discovery, dismissing antitrust lawsuits brought by 12 states and the Writers Guild as being less about competition and more about trust. Writing in an op-ed for The New York Times, Ellison said, “I believe this fight is not really about market share…The issue is whether I can be trusted as a steward of Warner’s CNN.” Ellison rejected speculation about his political leanings, noting he has supported candidates from both parties and holds a mix conservative and liberal views. He stressed that newsroom coverage under Warner would remain independent and fact-based. “Our journalists will continue to answer to the facts and to all the people they serve — not to any party or cause,” he wrote.Ellison has also revealed that he has outlined a plan to revive Hollywood by expanding Paramount’s theatrical and streaming output. Before the merger of Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. the company doubled its theatrical slate to 15 films, greenlit 40 Paramount+ series, and planned 90 TV series for 2026, while boosting content spending by $1.5 billion.After the merger happened, the combined company now aims to produce 30 theatrical films and 170 TV series annually, investing more than $30 billion in content each year. “Hollywood’s story can have a happy ending only when we connect with our audience,” Ellison said.A federal judge has scheduled the antitrust trial for March 2, 2027 which will delay the Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. merger by seven months. The lawsuit seeks to block the deal and this delay could cost Paramount over $1 billion in ticking fees, as it owes Warner Bros. Discovery shareholders about $7 million per day after September 30 if the merger remains unfinished. Ellison said the company is open to resolving the matter out of court but remains confident it will prevail at trial.Paramount Skydance reported mixed second-quarter results, with revenue rising 1% year-over-year to $6.91 billion, beating estimates, while profit fell short at $41 million. Streaming revenue grew 9% to nearly $2.5 billion, driven by subscriber gains from Paramount+ content including UFC Freedom 250 and the FIFA World Cup. Studio revenue reached $1.3 billion, though theatrical performance lagged compared to last year’s Mission: Impossible — The Final Reckoning.

Article Title: How Google's AI power centre has moved to Sergey Brin's desk after Demis Hassabis steps back from DeepMind
Article Text:
Demis Hassabis moves to chair as Sergey Brin's Mountain View orbit takes over Google's Gemini strategy.

Sergey Brin's return to Google AI began quietly in 2023 and never really stopped

Why Demis Hassabis is stepping back from Google DeepMind now

What Sergey Brin's influence means for London and the DeepMind research culture

Google's Gemini strategy now runs on shipping speed, not research prestige

For more than a decade, the most important desk in Google 's artificial intelligence operation sat in London. It belonged to Sir Demis Hassabis, the chess prodigy turned neuroscientist who sold DeepMind to Google in 2014 for around £400 million and then spent years defending it as a research lab first and a product factory second. That arrangement ended this week. Hassabis is stepping back from running Google DeepMind to become its chair and Alphabet's chief scientist, and day-to-day control of the lab passes to Koray Kavukcuoglu, the former DeepMind CTO now promoted to senior vice-president reporting directly to Sundar Pichai The seating chart says more than the press release does. According to the Financial Times, Kavukcuoglu moved from London to Mountain View last year and now leads Gemini development from a desk beside Sergey Brin . Google's co-founder holds no formal executive title, has not held one since 2019, and has still become one of the loudest voices on AI strategy inside a $4.4 trillion company. The power centre of Google AI has not just crossed the Atlantic. It has parked itself next to a man who told an I/O audience he comes into the office pretty much every day because he likes being deep in the technical details.Brin's re-entry was not an announcement. The Wall Street Journal reported in mid-2023 that he was turning up at Google's Charleston East building three or four days a week, sitting with the researchers building Gemini and arguing about loss curves.He convened weekly research discussions. He weighed in on which researchers to hire. Google said at the time that he had no new role beyond co-founder and board member, which was accurate and also beside the point. Three years on, the person overseeing Google's flagship model reports to Pichai and works within earshot of Brin, while the Nobel laureate who built the lab advises from London.Hassabis framed the move as a choice, and it did not happen overnight. People familiar with the reorganisation say the transition had been planned for months, with Hassabis handing over operational responsibility for Gemini development to Kavukcuoglu across the past year as Google accelerated work on its flagship models. Kavukcuoglu has also been reporting directly to Pichai since June. By the time Wednesday's announcement landed, much of the actual power had already changed hands.He told staff he wants the time and space to focus on the big picture and to shape what comes next in artificial general intelligence, which he said is "close at hand". He will also lean harder into Isomorphic Labs, the Alphabet drug discovery unit he founded in 2021, which has signed pharma partnerships but has yet to put an AI-designed drug into clinical trials.People inside the company tell a less tidy version. The FT reported that senior executives had grown frustrated by what they saw as his lighter interest in the commercial demands of the AI business, and that his decision to release AlphaFold freely—the work that won him the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry—became a source of internal tension because it returned little against the money spent on it. A person close to the company disputed that there was any friction, noting Hassabis led the original Gemini launch and is invested in its success.Bloomberg framed the reorganisation as the end of something larger: Hassabis was the only executive running a US tech giant's AI development from outside the country, and now nobody is. He resisted overtures to relocate to California for years. Early investor Frank Meehan told Bloomberg that Hassabis simply believes the UK can build the best AI companies. British AI minister Kanishka Narayan reportedly made Hassabis his first call after taking the job.Inside the London lab, the reaction has been jumpier. The FT quoted current and former DeepMind staff who fear the reorganisation marks the end of the research culture Hassabis protected, and one former executive at a rival firm said he had already fielded calls from people ready to move. Recruiters noticed within hours. Bloomberg reported that DeepMind staffers were posting on X about pitches from Prometheus Labs, Jeff Bezos's AI startup, that referenced the shakeup directly.The commercial context is unforgiving. Alphabet is spending upwards of $200 billion this year and posted negative free cash flow in Q2 for the first time since going public. Gemini has 950 million monthly users and Gemma has passed 900 million downloads, yet Google trails Anthropic and OpenAI on coding agents and enterprise deployment—the two places enterprise money is actually moving. John Jumper, who shared the Nobel with Hassabis, has already left for Anthropic. Noam Shazeer went to OpenAI. Alphabet shares fell around 5 per cent on the news.Kavukcuoglu's brief is narrow and brutal: ship faster. Whether he gets to do it on his own terms, with Brin a few feet away, is the question Google has not answered.
Article Summary: Demis Hassabis is stepping back from running Google DeepMind to become its chair and Alphabet's chief scientist. Day-to-day control of the lab passes to Koray Kavukcuoglu, the former DeepMind CTO now promoted to senior vice-president reporting directly to Sundar Pichai.

Article Title: Google Deepmind engineer lists five things that hint at how 'impossible' it is for OpenAI to survive more than two years, Sam Altman responds

Here’s what OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said

I am hypothesizing that for OpenAl to survive for longer than two years, it will have to (in no particular order):

Article Title: On National Handloom Day, study 'shows' wash anxiety around India’s handloom fabrics
Article Text:
Nadia: An artisan weaves on a traditional handloom at a rural workshop, a day ahead of National Handloom Day, in Nadia district, West Bengal. (PTI Photo)(PTI08_06_2026_000259A)

On the occasion of National Handloom Day, the Appliances Business of Godrej Enterprises Group has unveiled findings from its 'Handloom Dilemma’, a consumer survey conducted in partnership with Twentify India, which studied the usage, attitude and awareness of Indians with respect to handlooms revealing a gap between the consumers' stated love for India's handloom fabrics versus their actual awareness and usage.Handlooms are a symbol of India's diverse culture and heritage, representing centuries of regional artistry. The 'Handloom Dilemma Study' reveals that nearly 80% of Indians claim to love handlooms and are, in fact, more drawn towards these fabrics today than earlier. Considering their love for handlooms, 70% continue to rely on hand-washing or dry cleaning, driven by wash anxiety and the fear of damaging these delicate fabrics during washing. The need for greater confidence is evident, with 55% of consumers saying they want proof that a washing machine has been tested on handloom fabrics before trusting it with their cherished weaves. In a surprising finding, Gen Z shows a stronger love for handlooms than Gen X, reflecting growing interest in these handlooms.Despite the love, lack of awareness (echoed by 81%) and fabric care worries plague consumers. Perhaps this is why handloom is still seen foremost as occasion wear - coming out of the wardrobe mostly on the big days: family functions (71%), festivals (69%), temple visits (67%), weddings (64%) rather than regular days (36%). These are largely occasion clothes, tied to the moments that matter most. The thought of damaging a delicate weave during washing is perhaps enough to keep their favourite handloom sari or shirt or kurta safely tucked away in the wardrobe.The study, however, points towards an encouraging opportunity. An overwhelming 97% say they would wear and buy more handloom if washing it were easier and safer.
Article Summary: Handlooms are a symbol of India's diverse culture and heritage. Nearly 80% of Indians claim to love handlooms. 70% continue to rely on hand-washing or dry cleaning, driven by wash anxiety. Gen Z shows a stronger love for handloom than Gen X.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Sundar Pichai: “You might fail a few times, but that’s okay…” - what his words teach us about failure, learning and moving forward
Article Text:
PC: BBC

Quote of the day by Sundar Pichai

“You might fail a few times, but that's okay. You end up doing something worthwhile which you learn a great deal from”

What Sundar Pichai’s words actually mean

Sundar Pichai’s journey from Madurai to Google CEO

Why failure can produce useful information

What to do after failure: Lessons that help you move forward

What was within your control? What was not? Was the problem a lack of preparation, an unrealistic expectation, poor timing or simply an outcome that could not reasonably have been predicted?

Why the message still has relevance

What Sundar Pichai’s quote really teaches us about failure

Failure is not the end: An unsuccessful attempt does not necessarily mean the journey is over.

An unsuccessful attempt does not necessarily mean the journey is over. Every setback can teach you something: Even when things go wrong, the experience may provide useful knowledge for the future.

Even when things go wrong, the experience may provide useful knowledge for the future. Focus on what changed: Instead of asking only whether you succeeded or failed, consider what the experience taught you.

Instead of asking only whether you succeeded or failed, consider what the experience taught you. Learn from your mistakes: A setback can reveal weaknesses in your preparation, planning, timing or decision-making.

A setback can reveal weaknesses in your preparation, planning, timing or decision-making. Be willing to change direction: Failure may show that a particular approach or path is not worth pursuing further.

Failure may show that a particular approach or path is not worth pursuing further. Use experience to make better choices: What you learn from one attempt can influence how you approach the next one.

What you learn from one attempt can influence how you approach the next one. Failure does not guarantee success: Pichai’s words are not a promise that every mistake will eventually produce a positive outcome.

Pichai’s words are not a promise that every mistake will eventually produce a positive outcome. What happens next matters: Failure is simply an outcome; its longer-term value depends on how you respond and what you learn from it.

Failure tends to look much larger when it is happening to you than when you hear about it afterwards. A rejected application, an exam result that falls short or a project that quietly goes nowhere can feel like a dead end. Yet successful careers are rarely made up of clean decisions and predictable outcomes. Sundar Pichai , the Indian-born technology executive who became chief executive of Google and later Alphabet, has spoken about this in fairly plain terms. “You might fail a few times, but that's okay. You end up doing something worthwhile which you learn a great deal from,” he once said. The thought is less about celebrating failure than recognising what can remain after it.There is a tendency to divide experiences into success and failure, as if the two are fixed categories. Pichai’s observation is more useful when viewed as a description of a process.A failed attempt is an outcome. Learning is what comes after it.For instance, someone applying for a job and being turned down.The rejection may reveal very little. Or, after looking back at the interview, the applicant might realise that they struggled to explain their experience clearly. They can work on that before the next interview. The first application has not produced the desired result, but it has supplied something that can be used.The same applies outside work. A student who performs badly in an examination may discover that reading notes repeatedly was not an effective way of preparing. Someone starting a small business may learn that customers were interested in a product but unwilling to pay the planned price. A person learning a new skill may realise that their expectations were unrealistic.None of these situations becomes successful simply because a lesson can be extracted from it. The point is narrower: an unsuccessful outcome does not have to be the end of the useful part of the experience.Sundar Pichai was born in Madurai and grew up in Chennai. He studied metallurgical engineering at the Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur before moving to the United States for further education, including a master’s degree at Stanford University and an MBA at the Wharton School.He joined Google in 2004. His early work included responsibility for products associated with the company’s toolbar business and later Chrome, the web browser that became one of Google’s most recognisable products.His career inside the company developed over a number of years rather than through one sudden leap. He moved into increasingly senior roles, eventually becoming chief executive of Google in 2015. Four years later, he became chief executive of Alphabet, Google's parent company.That progression matters when considering his comments about failure. His career is often reduced to its most visible milestones, but those milestones were built through a succession of jobs, projects and decisions. A senior executive’s career, like anyone else’s, contains periods where the outcome of a decision cannot be known in advance.There is a practical side to Pichai’s observation. When an attempt succeeds immediately, there may be little incentive to examine every detail of what happened. Failure tends to force a closer look. That examination can be uncomfortable. It may uncover a gap in knowledge or a poor assumption. It can also expose circumstances that were outside a person’s control. Knowing which is which matters.A useful lesson is not necessarily a grand one. Perhaps a presentation needed more preparation. Perhaps an application was aimed at the wrong role. Perhaps a business idea needed testing before money was invested in it. Small discoveries can have a considerable effect when they influence the next decision.There is also a difference between learning from failure and simply experiencing it repeatedly. If the same problem keeps appearing and nothing changes, the setback itself has not taught very much. Pichai’s point depends on the second step: paying attention.The practical response to a setback need not be complicated. It can begin with a straightforward review of what happened.The answers are more useful than simply labelling the experience a failure. For a student, that might mean changing revision methods rather than merely spending more hours studying. For someone looking for employment, it could mean asking whether their applications are reaching the right roles or whether their interview answers need work. In a workplace, a project that did not deliver its intended result might lead to changes in planning, communication or testing.The useful habit is to carry something forward. Even a small adjustment gives the next attempt a different starting point.The pressure to appear successful can make ordinary setbacks feel more unusual than they really are. Professional networking sites, social media profiles and company announcements tend to present finished achievements. They rarely document every abandoned plan or unsuccessful first attempt that preceded them.For students and people early in their careers, that can create an incomplete picture of how progress happens. A CV records qualifications and positions, not every interview that did not work out or every project that was quietly shelved.Pichai’s comment offers a more modest way of looking at those experiences. A setback can be disappointing without being meaningless. It can also be useful without needing to be turned into a success story.That distinction is probably the most practical part of the quote.
Article Summary: Sundar Pichai, the Indian-born technology executive who became chief executive of Google and later Alphabet, has spoken about this in fairly plain terms. “You might fail a few times, but that's okay. You end up doing something worthwhile which you learn a great deal from,” he once said.

Article Title: WhatsApp banned 5.1 million accounts in June: Here’s what can get your account banned
Article Text:
WhatsApp account ban

Why WhatsApp bans an account

What can get your WhatsApp account banned

What a WhatsApp ban actually locks you out of

How to appeal a WhatsApp account ban

Meta recently admitted that a WhatsApp glitch wrongly locked out legitimate users recently, after its automatic content moderation system mistook normal account activity for spam or abusive behaviour. Earlier this month, multiple WhatsApp accounts were put under review for over 24 hours in several countries, prompting affected users to flag the issue on social media. Many reported seeing this message on their screen: "Account in review. Date requested: 3 Aug 2026. Your account activity and device info is being checked to make sure it follows our terms of service. We will notify you of the result typically within 24 hours."In a statement to TechCrunch, a Meta spokesperson confirmed the locks were an error, not a rule violation. The spokesperson said the company is constantly trying to identify fraudulent accounts to keep the platform safe, but acknowledged that "mistakes can occur." "Our goal is always to be one step ahead of those who want to abuse our service to ban accounts so that everyone can use it safely, sometimes we miss the mark and when we do, we work to remedy it as soon as possible to get everyone back to chatting," the spokesperson added.The scale of WhatsApp's moderation gives context to how something like this happens. In June alone this year, WhatsApp banned 5.1 million accounts in India — a volume of automated enforcement large enough that legitimate accounts can occasionally get caught in the net alongside genuine bad actors.WhatsApp says it bans accounts whose activity violates its Terms of Service — most commonly spam, scams, or behaviour that compromises other users' security. "We ban an account if we believe its activity violates our Terms of Service. For example, if an account is engaging in spam or scams, or if it compromises the security of WhatsApp users," the company states on its official FAQ page.Temporary bans work differently and have narrower causes. One is using an unofficial, third-party version of WhatsApp — apps that imitate the platform but aren't supported by the company because it cannot verify their security protocols. The other is "scraping," which WhatsApp defines as the automated collection of user information, either individually or at scale, for purposes not permitted on the platform. This can include harvesting phone numbers, profile photos, and status updates without consent.WhatsApp says users hit with a temporary ban for either reason should switch to the official app or stop scraping immediately. Continuing the behaviour, the company warns, can escalate a temporary restriction into a permanent ban.But as this month's incident shows, a restriction doesn't always mean a rule was actually broken. Meta itself has now acknowledged that its automated systems can misidentify legitimate accounts as spam or abusive — resulting in real users being locked out through no fault of their own.A permanently banned account shows the message "This account can't use WhatsApp" when the user opens the app. The impact goes beyond simply being unable to send or receive messages — WhatsApp says users also lose access to their chat history and backups while the ban is in place. Backups tied to the affected phone number remain inaccessible until that number is unbanned.A temporary restriction, as seen in this month's incident, can work differently — some users were simply told their account was under review while WhatsApp checked their activity and device information against its Terms of Service, rather than being locked out outright.Where the option is available, users can open WhatsApp and tap "Send review request." WhatsApp says it will examine the account and send a notification once a decision has been made. Users can track the status of their request from within the app itself.The company reviews only one phone number per appeal, and says contacting it repeatedly during the review — or using someone else's account to follow up — will not speed up the process or change the outcome. If no review option appears at all, WhatsApp treats the ban as permanent and non-appealable through this process.WhatsApp also warns users against paying third-party services that claim they can restore banned accounts, stating plainly that such services have no ability to ban or unban an account. Only WhatsApp itself can lift a restriction and restore access.For now, Meta hasn't detailed how many users worldwide were affected by the glitch or confirmed whether a fix has fully rolled out — so anyone still seeing "Account in review" beyond the stated 24-hour window may be better served trying the in-app appeal than simply waiting it out.
Article Summary: WhatsApp's automated moderation system can lock out legitimate users. This month, multiple accounts were locked out for over 24 hours in several countries. WhatsApp says it bans accounts whose activity violates its Terms of Service. But a temporary restriction doesn't always mean a rule was actually broken.

Article Title: 6 changes coming to Ask Maps on Google Maps in India
Article Text:
Google launches update for Ask Maps

Native Hindi language support

Personalised context via Gmail integration

Ability to resume past conversations

Real-time crowd, weather and traffic information

Live public transit widget

Curated venue and experience discovery

Google has announced updates to “Ask Maps,” its AI-powered conversational feature within Google Maps, bringing Hindi language support, real-time public transit tracking and personalised itinerary planning to millions of users across India. Powered by Google's Gemini models, the upgrade marks one of the most significant transformations to the navigation service in over a decade, allowing users to ask complex, real-world questions and receive tailored local insights.Following an initial rollout in India and the US, the six key features rolling out to enhance daily navigation and travel planning across the country include:Ask Maps is rolling out full support for Hindi. Users can type or speak queries naturally in Hindi to discover nearby places, plan driving routes, get local venue reviews, and ask for travel recommendations without needing to switch to English.Through a new feature called Personal Intelligence, users can choose to securely link Ask Maps with their Gmail accounts (and soon Google Calendar). When connected, Ask Maps automatically factors in upcoming flight bookings, hotel reservations, or restaurant confirmations.Ask Maps now maintains a conversational memory for users who have their history settings enabled.Travelers can now pick up where they left off during trip planning, essentially eliminating the need to re-enter preferences or start planning from scratch.The updated assistant delivers real-time context about destinations and routes. Users can check current traffic bottlenecks along their morning commute, review local weather conditions, or check live busyness levels at shops and restaurants before leaving home to avoid long wait times.Google is introducing a dedicated live transit widget directly inside the Ask Maps interface. The tool provides up-to-the-minute departure schedules, route updates, and delay alerts for local buses, metro systems, and trains.The updated capabilities allow for specific venue vetting based on individual preferences, for example, Users can prompt the app to find quiet restaurants suitable for business conversations or locate family-friendly venues with dedicated kids' play zones.
Article Summary: Google launches update for Ask Maps, its AI-powered conversational feature within Google Maps. Hindi language support, real-time public transit tracking and personalised itinerary planning. Powered by Google's Gemini models, the upgrade marks one of the most significant transformations to the navigation service in over a decade.

Article Title: Hacked AI email accounts can help attackers steal $250,000 through CEO fraud: Report
Article Text:
AI generated image for representation

How the attack unfolded

AI helped attackers compromise the CEO

Attackers also concealed the fraud

AI increases the speed of post-compromise attacks

Hacked artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled email accounts can accelerate cyberattacks. A new report from Barracuda's Red Team says attackers who gain access to AI-enabled business email accounts can use built-in AI assistants to identify sensitive information, impersonate executives and redirect payments. In a controlled proof-of-concept, researchers demonstrated how a compromised employee account could escalate into CEO fraud and lead to the theft of $247,500 (nearly $250,000) through a fraudulent wire transfer.The report says the risk does not stem from AI creating new privileges, but from helping attackers use the permissions they already have more quickly. By leveraging AI assistants such as Microsoft Copilot, attackers were able to automate reconnaissance, draft convincing phishing emails, establish persistence inside compromised accounts and carry out business email compromise (BEC) attacks.According to Barracuda, the simulated attack began after an attacker gained access to an employee's AI-enabled email account. Using the built-in AI assistant, the attacker first created inbox rules that automatically moved login notifications to the Deleted Items folder, reducing the victim's chances of detecting suspicious sign-ins.The AI assistant was then used to analyse emails, documents, calendar entries and organisational relationships to identify senior executives inside the company.Researchers said the compromised AI assistant also drafted a phishing email in the employee's writing style, which was sent to the CEO from the employee's legitimate mailbox.After the CEO clicked the phishing link, the attacker used an adversary-in-the-middle attack to steal the CEO's authenticated session token, granting access to the CEO's account and bypassing multi-factor authentication.The attackers then repeated the inbox rule tactic to suppress security notifications in the CEO's mailbox before using the AI assistant to summarise recent financial conversations.According to the report, a prompt requesting recent invoices, payment amounts, and upcoming transfers quickly surfaced a pending $247,500 wire transfer awaiting final approval.The AI assistant was then used to draft an email from the CEO's account requesting that the finance team update the recipient's bank account details before processing the payment.Because the message originated from the CEO's genuine mailbox, matched the executive's writing style and referenced an active transaction, the finance team updated the banking information and transferred the funds to an attacker-controlled account as part of the simulation.To prevent the CEO from seeing confirmation emails, the attackers created another inbox rule that automatically forwarded messages from the finance team to an attacker-controlled email address while hiding them from the CEO's inbox.The report also showed how the AI assistant could quickly identify emails related to the fraudulent transaction, allowing attackers to remove evidence more efficiently than through manual searches.Barracuda said the proof of concept demonstrates that AI assistants do not introduce new access rights but significantly increase the speed and scale at which attackers can exploit compromised accounts."The primary security risk posed by AI assistants is not that they create new privileges, but that they dramatically increase the speed, scale and effectiveness with which attackers can exploit the privileges they already obtain through account compromise," the report said.The company added that organisations should focus on preventing the initial account compromise while monitoring AI-enabled accounts for suspicious activity such as inbox rule abuse, persistence mechanisms and business email compromise attempts.According to Barracuda, securing AI-enabled email accounts should become a core part of enterprise identity and email security strategies as AI assistants become more widely integrated into workplace communication and business workflows.
Article Summary: Attackers can use built-in AI assistants to identify sensitive information, impersonate executives and redirect payments. Researchers demonstrated how a compromised employee account could escalate into CEO fraud and lead to the theft of $247,500 (nearly $250,000) through a fraudulent wire transfer.
