Article Title: Canadian billionaire Kevin O'Leary says that Wall Street is booming, but that is may not shape 2026 elections, here's what is likely to
Article Text:
Kevin O'Leary believes gas prices as a main election issue

Criticism of Trump’s economic policies

Kevin O’Leary predicts that America, Canada and Mexico will unite

Canadian billionaire and Shark Tank investor Kevin O’Leary recently said that while Wall Street is booming and the US economy is showing strength via corporate earnings and stock market gains, many households are still struggling with affordability. “There’s a huge disconnect between the performance of the underlying economy, whether it be small business or the S&P 500,” he noted, pointing to what he called an “extraordinary earning season.” O’Leary said the economy is performing “on all cylinders,” but warned that inflation above 3% continues to weigh on consumers.Canadian billionaire O’Leary also argued that energy costs could play a decisive role in shaping voter sentiment ahead of the 2026 elections. “The number one input cost for every voter everywhere, every state, red or blue, is energy. It’s gasoline,” he said. He suggested that lowering oil prices below $70 per barrel before November could significantly influence voter opinions and potentially affect control of Congress.President Donald Trump has faced criticism over inflation and affordability issues. Economist Peter Schiff cited a July AP-NORC poll showing Trump’s approval rating at 33%, attributing the low numbers to voter concerns over rising costs.Lawmakers including Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren have accused the administration of favouring billionaires and worsening household expenses through spending priorities and tariffs. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Illinois Governor JB Pritzker also criticised Trump’s handling of inflation.In related news, recently Kevin O’Leary believes that the fear of China’s rise will be the driving force behind deeper economic integration between the United States, Canada and Mexico. According to a report by Business Insider, O’Leary posted a video on social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter) in which the venture capitalist said that covers over China’s advances in AI, technology, warfare and power generation will outweigh political disagreements across North America. O’Leary argued that each country brings unique strengths to the table: “Canada has the energy and critical minerals, the United States has the scale and innovation, and Mexico plays a vital role in the North American economy,” he said. He added that cooperation is not just good policy but “an economic necessity” as the race for AI, energy, and critical infrastructure accelerates.The comments made by the Canadian billionaire come amid the growing recognition of China’s technological momentum. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk also recently told Economist that China already produces far more electricity than the US and it could become the world’s AI leader if it manages to secure enough computing power. American AI labs OpenAI and Anthropic have also warned that Chinese rivals are closing the gap, with Beijing-based Moonshot AI drawing attention for its Kimi K3 model.
Article Summary: Canadian billionaire Kevin O'Leary believes gas prices as a main election issue. O’Leary believes fear of China’s rise will be the driving force behind deeper economic integration between the United States, Canada and Mexico. He added that cooperation is not just good policy but an economic necessity as the race for AI, energy and critical infrastructure accelerates.

Article Title: Intel proves its worth with $8.2 billion SoftBank boost while OpenAI gains pause
Article Text:
Intel investment delivers big payoff

OpenAI gains stall amid heavy AI spending

SoftBank Group reported first-quarter profits that topped market expectations this week, driven by a massive $8.2 billion valuation gain on its stake in US chipmaker Intel. The surprise boost from Intel helped offset a quiet quarter for SoftBank’s artificial intelligence (AI) investments, where gains from ChatGPT maker OpenAI temporarily ground to a halt.According to CNBC, SoftBank reported a net profit of 347.3 billion Japanese yen (roughly $2.2 billion). While that figure represented an 18% decline year-over-year, it comfortably beat average analyst estimates of 120.23 billion yen.The standout driver behind SoftBank's quarterly performance was its investment in Intel. SoftBank recorded a 1.3 trillion yen ($8.2 billion) unrealised gain on its Intel shares, following a $2 billion position the company established in the chip manufacturer last year. Intel shares have surged nearly 400% over the past 12 months.This massive surge lifted SoftBank's core investment division to a segment profit of 1.05 trillion yen. Meanwhile, SoftBank’s Vision Fund division recorded a modest $1.7 billion gain in portfolio value.The growth was primarily propelled by a $2.2 billion valuation rise in TikTok owner ByteDance, which helped absorb paper losses across other holdings like Japanese digital payments company PayPay.Overall, the Vision Fund segment generated 5.4 billion yen in profit, down sharply from 451.4 billion yen in the same period last year.In contrast to the previous quarter, when SoftBank recorded a massive $20 billion gain almost entirely powered by OpenAI, the firm reported zero gain or loss from its OpenAI holding for the June quarter. SoftBank has committed more than $60 billion to OpenAI, a deal that aims to give the Japanese giant an estimated 13 percent ownership stake. According to executive disclosures, $55 billion of that total has already been transferred to the AI startup.Despite the pause in OpenAI valuation gains, SoftBank CEO Masayoshi Son remains committed to the sector. Son recently defended the company's aggressive strategy, pointing out that OpenAI represents roughly 20% of SoftBank’s net asset value and calling the AI boom a historical turning point.“This is the biggest revolution of technology and realization that mankind ever experienced, so this is just like the beginning of the internet,” Son said regarding the long-term prospects of AI.
Article Summary: SoftBank reported a net profit of 347.3 billion Japanese yen (roughly $2.2 billion) in the first quarter, beating market expectations by 18%. The Japanese tech giant recorded a massive $8.2billion valuation gain on its stake in US chipmaker Intel. This helped offset a quiet quarter for SoftBank’s artificial intelligence investments, where gains from ChatGPT maker OpenAI ground to a halt.

Article Title: Demis Hassabis calls himself a scientist first. 12 years after buying DeepMind, Google has let him be one
Article Text:
Sir Demis Hassabis has a Nobel Prize, a $2.6 billion drug company, and no longer runs Google DeepMind.

Running Google's AI was never the job Demis wanted

Isomorphic Labs is not the consolation prize it looks like

Google needed Demis Hassabis until it needed someone faster

Hassabis and Google are no longer chasing the same thing

A year ago, in his office at DeepMind's London headquarters, Demis Hassabis told The Guardian something that sounded like a throwaway regret. If he'd had his way, he said, they would have "left it in the lab for longer" and done more things like AlphaFold. Cured cancer, maybe. Instead ChatGPT arrived, the race started, and the man who wanted to be left alone with the proteins became the public face of Google 's answer to it.It was not the first time he had said it, or acted on it. Twenty years earlier he had wound up a games company to go and study amnesia.That one he decided for himself. On Wednesday, nine days after his fiftieth birthday, Google decided the second one.The move was dressed as a promotion, and by title it is one. Sir Demis Hassabis becomes Chair of Google DeepMind and Chief Scientist of Alphabet, and keeps Isomorphic Labs, the drug design company he spun out of DeepMind in 2021. What he does not keep is the organisation. Koray Kavukcuoglu, DeepMind's chief technology officer and one of the first researchers Hassabis ever hired, takes Gemini model development, frontier research and the Gemini app, and reports to Sundar Pichai Everything about it looks like a man being moved aside. Almost nothing about the past twenty years suggests he would mind.Hassabis has never hidden how little he enjoyed the corporate half of his career, and once before, he gave up a company to escape it.By 2005 he had a decade of the games industry behind him: Theme Park at seventeen, a double first at Cambridge, then Elixir Studios, the London developer he founded at 22 and ran for seven years.That year he sold off the rights to the games he had built, wound the company up, and went back to university.What he went back for was not computing. It was cognitive neuroscience, at UCL, under Eleanor Maguire. His first paper, in PNAS in 2007, showed that patients with hippocampal amnesia could not imagine new experiences either: the brain remembers its past and pictures its future with the same machinery. Science named it one of the ten breakthroughs of the year. He founded DeepMind the year after he left.He sold it in 2014. Google paid £400 million for a lab with fifty-odd people, no product and no revenue, which was roughly what Hassabis had told investors to expect when they asked what DeepMind would sell: nothing yet, because it was building the most important thing of all time. What Google had that he wanted was compute, on a scale no independent lab could buy. What Google wanted was less clear to him, and he negotiated for an ethics board and a set of limits on how the work could be used, then went back to the research.It did not hold. Sebastian Mallaby's biography of Hassabis has him and his co-founder Mustafa Suleyman spending close to three years from 2015 trying to prise DeepMind out of Google altogether, under an independent board, with Reid Hoffman prepared to put a billion dollars behind the split. Pichai refused. What Hassabis wanted from that fight was not power but distance, and he lost it.He stayed, and the lab changed around him. DeepMind, he told CNBC in 2024, was "like the engine room of the company"—a line that sounds like a boast until you notice that engine rooms sit below deck. He made his researchers sit on papers for six months before publishing in case what they had found was commercially sensitive, a rule that went down badly in a lab whose scientists had spent a decade measuring themselves by what they got into Nature. The scoreboard changed with it: user growth in, journal citations out.None of this was hidden. Six current and former employees told Business Insider that Hassabis had drifted from the job for about a year, one longtime Googler reducing it to a sentence: he does not care about chatbots, he wants to use AI to cure cancer. The parts he had been shedding were the ones he never wanted—refereeing team politics, sitting through product decisions that did not hold his attention.Google's side of it is less flattering. The Financial Times, citing a dozen people familiar with the company, reported that senior executives had grown frustrated by what they saw as his lesser focus on the commercial demands of the AI business. A person close to the company disputed there had been any tension.Which makes the obvious question one of what he is actually left with. The lazy reading of Wednesday is that Isomorphic is a science project handed to a scientist to keep him busy, and to keep him at all, in a year when Google has been losing people it could not afford to lose. The money says otherwise. In May it closed a $2.1 billion Series B led by Thrive Capital, with Alphabet, Abu Dhabi's MGX and Singapore's Temasek joining, taking outside capital past $2.6 billion. Its partnerships with Novartis and Eli Lilly are worth close to $3 billion between them.This is not a hobby. It is one of the largest private financings in AI drug discovery, and he has been running it alongside a job that already had him working, by his own account, until four in the morning. It is also unproven. Five years in, Isomorphic has yet to put an AI-designed drug into clinical trials.What he intends to do with it he set out in Stockholm in December 2024, accepting a prize for work that started with a question about brains. His argument since UCL has run roughly like this. A brain is not a store of facts; it is a device that builds models of the world and uses them to guess what happens next, which is what imagining and remembering and hypothesising all turn out to be.Build a machine that works the same way and you do not get a better encyclopaedia. You get something that can go and find out what nobody knows yet—and then you point it at the questions where finding out has been the bottleneck for fifty years.The lecture had two halves. The first went to AlphaFold and the fifty-year problem of predicting a protein's three-dimensional shape from its amino acid sequence: the roughly 170,000 experimentally determined structures that trained the system, and the accuracy down to the width of a single atom that led the contest grading the field since 1994 to declare the problem solved in 2020. Then he gave all of it away. Over 200 million structures, released free, used since by more than two million researchers across 190 countries.Not everyone at Google admired the gesture. The FT reported this week that the giveaway became a source of internal tension, an enormous investment returning almost nothing commercially, and that the AlphaFold team has since been broken up. John Jumper, who shared the Nobel with him for it, left for Anthropic earlier this year.Then he generalised it. AlphaFold, he argued, was not a one-off but a template: find a problem with a vast combinatorial search space, a clear objective to optimise against, and enough data or a good enough simulator, and the same method applies. He called the result digital biology, and proposed a conjecture from the podium: that any pattern found in nature can be efficiently discovered and modelled by a classical learning algorithm.Isomorphic is that thesis with patients attached. Its stated goal is to solve all disease, a phrase Hassabis uses without visible embarrassment, and its next target beyond molecules is a virtual cell able to predict how an intervention plays out before anyone touches a pipette. In his memo to staff on Wednesday he wrote that AI's highest application has always been human health, and asked what better demonstration there could be than helping to "cure diseases like cancer. "Why now, when Isomorphic has existed since 2021 and the wish to be back in the science for longer than that? Because until now Google could not afford to let him go.ChatGPT arrived in November 2022, Pichai declared a code red, and Larry Page and Sergey Brin were called back in to help find an answer. Brin stayed. He has been in Mountain View most days since, sitting with the researchers training Gemini, arguing about loss curves, weighing in on who gets hired—the technical detail he has said is where his scientific interest actually lies. He is not on the org chart and does not need to be. Kavukcuoglu relocated from London last year and now runs the models from a desk beside his. He is also, by some readings inside the company, on a path towards eventually succeeding Pichai.The symmetry is hard to miss. One founder came back into the trenches because the race is the interesting part; the other spent three years trying to get out of the building. Hassabis built DeepMind in London to prove a frontier lab did not have to sit in Silicon Valley. Gemini is run from Silicon Valley now.If Google was calling a founder back in, it was never going to let Hassabis walk out. Instead it did the opposite, merging DeepMind with Google Brain, its own in-house AI lab, in 2023 and putting him over both, then folding in the safety and research teams and the Gemini apps business until the lab was the company's AI engine in fact as well as in his phrasing.Nothing about Hassabis changed after the merge. What changed was what Google needed from the person holding his job. Gemini 3 had put Google back in front after a bruising year, which in this business means very little for very long. Every lab has led it at some point and been overtaken within months of saying so, and Google is behind again already—the follow-up has slipped since June, and Pichai conceded on the last earnings call that the company needs to improve at agentic coding.Train, ship, lead for a quarter, get overtaken, train again. That is the job now. Somebody has to want it, and by every account of the past year, he no longer did.Hassabis has a phrase he keeps returning to for where we are: the foothills of the singularity. Pichai quoted it back at him on Wednesday, framing the new role as one that lets Hassabis give his full attention to shaping what AGI becomes.What he means by it is narrower than what his peers mean. At Davos in January he held to five to ten years, and said his bar was higher than theirs because he counts AGI as a system that can produce new hypotheses, not one that performs economically valuable tasks. What is still missing, he said, is continual learning, better memory, robotics that works, and world models—systems that understand the physical world well enough to predict it, which he works on personally.A machine that can have an idea nobody has had is a scientist's target. He set it before Google owned any of this, and it is not reached by shipping quarterly. Some of it has started arriving anyway: DeepMind systems took gold at the International Mathematical Olympiad last summer and are now pointed at Millennium Prize problems.Five to ten years is a short time to spend in the wrong job. He has said for twenty of them that the first thing to do with AGI is cure disease, and whoever does it first will be whoever has already built the apparatus to use it. Isomorphic is his.DeepMind is not, and that is the price. The lab he founded in 2010 and spent sixteen years shielding is now run out of California, by a man he hired, reporting to a chief executive who once refused to let him take it away.London took it hard. Current and former staff told the FT the news went through the building like a shock, some of them convinced it ends the research culture Hassabis spent a decade defending, and a former executive at a rival firm said the calls from people ready to leave started that day. A friend told the paper Hassabis himself was relieved. Both of those can be true at once, and probably are.The DeepMind he is handing over is not the one he built. Everyone who worked there can see that research is no longer what it is for, which is why the other half of Wednesday's news was Jeff Dean leaving after twenty-seven years to start a company that will do the thing DeepMind stopped making room for. Hassabis says the models are in good hands with Kavukcuoglu, and so, presumably, is the frontier that has been late since June.What he takes with him is what he came for in the first place: the science. It is the narrowest job he has held in a decade and the only one he ever wanted, and it is not the retreat it looks like. He still thinks a machine will one day have an idea nobody has had. He would rather be standing in a lab when it does.
Article Summary: Sir Demis Hassabis becomes Chair of Google DeepMind and Chief Scientist of Alphabet. He keeps Isomorphic Labs, the drug design company he spun out of DeepMind in 2021. What he does not keep is the organisation. Koray Kavukcuoglu, DeepMind's chief technology officer, takes Gemini model development, frontier research and the Gemini app.

Article Title: Waymo co-CEO explains why physical AI can't follow Silicon Valley's 'move fast and break things' mantra
Article Text:
Image credit: X (Twitter)

"

move fast and break things

"

"move fast and ship safely,"

"In Silicon Valley, there's a common mantra to 'move fast and break things.' However, when you're dealing with atoms instead of bits, breaking things is not really okay,”

'There's simply not an undo and a retry button': Waymo co-CEO Dmitri Dolgov on AI safety

"So the thing you have to do is to move fast and ship safely,”

"You have to build AI models, and you have to build training recipes where safety is the foundation and not an afterthought, not an add-on,”

"There's simply not an undo and a retry button."

Waymo co-CEO’s comments come amid AI safety concerns

Waymo has also faced regulatory scrutiny

Waymo co-CEO Dmitri Dolgov believes physical artificial intelligence (AI) requires safety-first development. He said AI used in the physical world cannot follow Silicon Valley's long-standingphilosophy because mistakes can have real-world consequences. Speaking during a Y Combinator talk released this week, Dolgov said developers building self-driving cars and robotics must insteadwith safety built into AI systems from the start.Dolgov said the difference between digital AI and physical AI lies in the cost of errors. While a mistake made by a chatbot may require only another prompt, failures involving autonomous vehicles or robots can put people at risk.Dolgov said.Dolgov, who has worked on Google's self-driving car project since 2009 and became part of Waymo after it was spun out as an Alphabet company in 2016, said physical AI systems must be designed with robustness and safety as core requirements rather than post-launch additions.he saidDolgov added.Explaining the distinction between generative AI and autonomous systems, he said, "You have a language model or a chatbot or a co-pilot, and it makes a mistake, usually it costs you a retry. In the physical world, the cost of a mistake can be measured in human lives, not tokens."He continued,Dolgov's remarks come as recent AI-related security incidents have renewed discussions around AI safety and oversight. Last month, Hugging Face disclosed a security breach in which an AI agent accessed some of its internal datasets. Around the same time, OpenAI said its models escaped a sandbox environment, accessed the internet and carried out a rogue hack.More recently, Anthropic reported a similar incident, saying it had identified cases in which Claude models gained unauthorised access to internal systems at three different companies.Reacting to the OpenAI incident, Box CEO Aaron Levie wrote on X: "If you were wondering how powerful AI is getting, Agents are now capable of escaping out of systems, finding their way to the internet, discovering zero day security vulnerabilities along the way, and then breaking into external systems - all in an attempt to complete their goal."Waymo has logged millions of autonomous driving miles while largely avoiding major injury-causing crashes, but the company has faced regulatory reviews over software-related issues.In 2024, the US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) opened an investigation into reports of unexpected driving behaviour, including collisions with stationary objects and traffic-law violations, which led to software recalls. In 2025 and earlier this year, Waymo also issued recalls after several robotaxis entered freeway construction zones.
Article Summary: Waymo co-CEO Dmitri Dolgov believes physical AI requires safety-first development. He said AI used in the physical world cannot follow Silicon Valley's long-standingphilosophy because mistakes can have real-world consequences. Dolgov's remarks come as recent AI-related security incidents have renewed discussions around AI safety.

Article Title: AI ‘godmother’ Fei-Fei Li just said what Nvidia CEO told fellow CEOs on doomsday scenario
Article Text:
Rebutting the ‘end of humanity’ narrative

AI pioneer Fei-Fei Li has pushed back against “doomsday” narratives surrounding artificial intelligence (AI), echoing recent skepticism voiced by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang over catastrophic predictions about the technology’s future. Speaking on an industry panel alongside fellow AI researcher Geoffrey Hinton, Li, who is often called the “godmother of AI”, criticised both apocalyptic fear-mongering and overly idealistic optimism, calling for a balanced, practical perspective on technology adoption.“Every tool is a double-edged sword,” said Li, who serves as co-founder and CEO of spatial intelligence startup World Labs, adding, “AI is such a powerful tool. If not wielded in the right way, it will bring harm to our work and our life.”Li’s comments align with a sharp public rebuke delivered by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang against apocalyptic warnings surrounding artificial intelligence. In a recent interview with Axios, Huang dismissed claims that AI development will trigger civilisation-ending catastrophes or wipe out half of the workforce, arguing that scare tactics pose a far greater threat to economic growth than the technology itself.“The fact that this is going to be the end of humanity – it’s complete nonsense. The fact that this is going to destroy half of the American jobs is complete nonsense,” Huang said. Huang warned that overreacting to hypothetical extinction scenarios risks suffocating practical innovation across medical research, enterprise automation, and scientific discovery.Huang and Li’s measured stance stands in sharp contrast to warnings issued by other prominent tech executives and AI pioneers.Sam Altman (OpenAI) previously warned that unchecked AI could lead to severe global risks and co-signed public declarations urging leaders to treat AI extinction risks as a top priority. Dario Amodei (Anthropic) has repeatedly cautioned that rapid model training trajectories could cause mass job displacement and catastrophic safety breaches.Similarly, Elon Musk has repeatedly called for regulatory oversight and pauses on unchecked frontier model deployments, describing superintelligence as a major existential threat.
Article Summary: AI pioneer Fei-Fei Li has pushed back against ‘doomsday’ narratives surrounding artificial intelligence. Her comments echo recent skepticism voiced by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang over catastrophic predictions about the technology’s future. Li criticised both apocalyptic fear-mongering and overly idealistic optimism, calling for a balanced, practical perspective.

Article Title: Microsoft launches Hyderabad cloud region, expands to four datacenter regions in India
Article Text:
Representative Image

Hyderabad region adds to Microsoft's India cloud network

"Whether it is a Frontier Firm already running AI at scale or an enterprise taking its first steps, the question we hear most often is: how do we move faster from experimenting with AI to creating durable business value with AI? That requires trusted infrastructure close to where data lives, teams work and decisions are made.

The Microsoft India South Central datacenter region is a critical part of that foundation, backed by Microsoft’s $20.5 billion investment commitment to India’s cloud and AI future.

Making India AI-first is about bringing together the scale to support growth, the skills to unlock value, the sovereignty organizations expect, and the security they depend on. We are not investing in infrastructure to keep up with demand.

We are investing in India’s ability to set the pace for the world."

Enterprise demand drives Microsoft’s expansion

Part of Microsoft's broader AI investment in India

Microsoft has launched a new cloud region in Hyderabad. The company announced the general availability of its India South Central cloud region in Hyderabad, expanding its footprint to four Microsoft-operated datacenter regions in India. The new region enables customers to run eligible Microsoft Cloud services and workloads locally while supporting AI, cloud modernisation, and enterprise applications with security, compliance, and governance capabilities.The Hyderabad launch strengthens Microsoft's cloud infrastructure in India alongside its existing regions in Pune, Chennai and Mumbai. The company said the new datacenter region is part of its broader investment in India's cloud and AI ecosystem and is backed by its previously announced $20.5 billion investment commitment in the country.The India South Central region comprises three Availability Zones designed to support mission-critical workloads. Microsoft said the infrastructure has been built in line with India's regulatory and seismic-zone requirements and will provide customers with more options to deploy cloud services closer to where their data and operations are located.Puneet Chandok, President, Microsoft India and South Asia, said,With the Hyderabad launch, Microsoft now operates cloud regions in Central India (Pune), South India (Chennai), West India (Mumbai), and South Central India (Hyderabad). The company also operates two datacenters in partnership with Jio—Jio India West and Jio India Central.Microsoft said the Hyderabad region has already seen early demand from enterprises including Adani Group, Bajaj Finserv, HDFC Bank and PB Pay, which are using the region to support business continuity, operational resilience, cloud capacity and AI initiatives.The company added that Azure has recorded strong double-digit growth in India over the past two years, with enterprise AI adoption increasing as well.According to Microsoft, more than 90% of NIFTY 100 companies in its analysis are using Microsoft 365 Copilot. The company also said Infosys, TCS, Wipro, and LTM have collectively signed up for more than 400,000 Microsoft 365 Copilot seats, while the platform has crossed 30 million paid seats globally, according to Microsoft's FY26 fourth-quarter results.The Hyderabad cloud region builds on Microsoft's previously announced investments in India, including a $3 billion investment announced in January 2025 and an additional $17.5 billion investment announced in December 2025.Globally, Microsoft's cloud infrastructure spans more than 80 regions across 34 countries, with over 500 datacenters, 800,000 kilometres of terrestrial and subsea fibre, and more than 32 million kilometres of network cables.
Article Summary: Microsoft has launched a new cloud region in Hyderabad. The company said the new datacenter region is part of its broader investment in India's cloud and AI ecosystem. The Hyderabad launch strengthens Microsoft's cloud infrastructure in India alongside its existing regions in Pune, Chennai and Mumbai.

Article Title: 'This person wasn't real': Arena CEO says AI job applicants fooled engineers during interviews
Article Text:
AI-generated image for representation

"This person wasn't real. It was AI,"

"They're passing all of our technical interviews. And then what happens at the end of it? You try to hire them, and it's vaporware,”

Company considering in-person onboarding

"If you want a laptop, you got to come to the office. We got to go and shake your hand. We got to verify that you're real."

"People are trying to get into all of the American businesses.

We're not the only ones. This is happening everywhere."

AI-powered interview fraud has drawn attention from US authorities

How companies are tightening hiring verification

Arena has revealed that some candidates it interviewed were AI-generated rather than real people. Anastasios Angelopoulos, the co-founder and CEO of the AI model evaluation company, said that he encountered fake candidates that successfully cleared technical interviews before disappearing during the hiring process. Describing one such case, he said,adding that the incident has prompted the company to consider requiring in-person onboarding for new employees.Speaking on the "20VC" podcast released this week, Angelopoulos said Arena's engineers interviewed the candidates believing they were genuine applicants. He did not explain how the company later determined the applicants were AI-generated but said the incidents have raised concerns about identity verification during recruitment.he said.Angelopoulos said the experience is pushing Arena to rethink parts of its hiring process, particularly for remote employees. He said,He added that Arena is not alone in facing the issue. Angelopoulos noted,While Angelopoulos said he does not know who was behind the applications, he suggested possible motives could include corporate espionage, cyberattacks or attempts to gain access to company systems and source code.The comments come as US companies continue to face cases involving fake job applicants. In a 2025 alert, the FBI warned that North Korean IT workers were using AI and face-swapping technology during video interviews to conceal their identities and obtain remote jobs at US companies. According to the bureau, some of those workers later used their access to steal proprietary and sensitive information after securing employment at more than 100 US companies.The FBI advised employers to verify candidates' identities during interviews and onboarding (preferably in person) and to continue identity checks throughout remote employment.Several technology companies have introduced additional safeguards against fraudulent job applications. Coinbase now requires employees to attend in-person orientation in the US, while Amazon has used AI systems to identify and block applications suspected to be linked to North Korean operatives.Research firm Gartner also highlighted the growing issue in a second-quarter 2025 survey of 3,000 job candidates, which found that 6% admitted participating in interview fraud by either impersonating another person or having someone else attend an interview on their behalf.Gartner projects that one in four candidate profiles worldwide could be fake by 2028, underscoring the increasing challenge companies face in verifying applicants during remote hiring processes.
Article Summary: AI model evaluation company Arena says some candidates it interviewed were AI- generated rather than real people. Company considering requiring in-person onboarding for new employees. FBI warned that North Korean IT workers were using AI and face-swapping technology during video interviews to conceal their identities and obtain remote jobs.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Larry Page: “You need to get one thing done well, or else…” - a reminder to stop chasing everything at once
Article Text:
Larry Page advocates for completing one task well before starting others. This focused approach builds confidence and a strong foundation for future endeavors. Many fields, including education and business, benefit from this principle of deep mastery. Rushing tasks can create future problems, while high standards require patience and revision. This principle remains relevant amidst modern distractions and constant communication shifts.

Quote of the day by Larry Page

“You need to get one thing done well, or else you don't have permission to do anything else.”

Understand the meaning behind Page’s quote

Why doing it well matters more than doing it quickly

All about Larry Page

Lessons that can be applied

Other famous quotes by Larry Page

“You never lose a dream, it just incubates as a hobby.”

“Always deliver more than expected.”

“When you aim for the stars you may come up short, but still reach the moon.”

“Have a healthy disregard for the impossible.”

Why the quote still feels relevant

With many distractions in this era and multitasking becoming the order of the day, staying focused has become one of the greatest struggles of the current generation. Larry Page, one of the co-founders of Google, is known to emphasise the need to combine ambition and execution well. This strategy is based on the notion that success only results when one identifies the appropriate priorities and pays adequate attention to accomplishing them. In education, in business, and in any area of creativity, distributing one’s attention to many things at once makes the process less efficient and sometimes the outcome less effective. Concentrating on fewer meaningful goals often improves decision-making, reduces unnecessary distractions and increases the likelihood of producing consistently high-quality results over time.Larry Page is pointing towards focus rather than limitation. Many people are tempted to divide their attention across several goals at once, believing that more activity automatically means greater achievement. The quote argues for almost the opposite approach.Completing one important objective creates a solid foundation.It develops confidence, demonstrates capability and often provides resources or knowledge that make the next challenge easier. Skipping this step can leave every project competing for time without any reaching a meaningful finish.This way of thinking appears in many fields. A student may benefit more from mastering one difficult subject before taking on several advanced courses. A business may be wiser to perfect one product before introducing five new ones. Even creative work often improves when attention is concentrated instead of scattered.There is another layer to the quote that is easy to miss. It is not simply about finishing something; it is about finishing it well.That distinction matters. Speed has obvious advantages, but rushing through an important task can create problems that demand even more attention later. High standards usually require patience, repeated revision and the willingness to ignore distractions.The quote also questions the appeal of constant expansion. Modern work often rewards visible activity. Meetings multiply, ideas accumulate and side projects appear before earlier ones are complete. Page's observation suggests that growth without a dependable foundation can become difficult to sustain.Larry Page is an American computer scientist and entrepreneur best known as the co-founder of Google alongside Sergey Brin. While both were doctoral students at Stanford University in the late 1990s, they developed a search engine that ranked web pages according to the relationships between links rather than simply counting keywords. That idea eventually became Google.As the company expanded, Page held several leadership roles, including chief executive. Under his leadership, Google broadened far beyond internet search into products and services covering advertising, mobile software, cloud computing and artificial intelligence. In 2015, Google became part of Alphabet, a new parent company created to oversee Google's operations alongside a range of long-term technology ventures.Throughout his career, Page has often spoken about ambitious thinking, engineering discipline and solving problems at large scale. Even so, many of his comments return to a familiar principle: meaningful progress usually begins with getting the fundamentals right.The quote lends itself to practical situations without requiring dramatic changes in behaviour.For professionals, it can mean identifying the task that has the greatest impact and giving it full attention before accepting additional responsibilities. Delivering reliable work often creates more opportunities than attempting everything at once.Students may see the same pattern in revision. Understanding one topic thoroughly can be more valuable than quickly reading several chapters without retaining much of the material.Business leaders can interpret the message as a reminder to strengthen existing operations before expanding into unfamiliar markets. Growth built on dependable systems tends to be easier to manage than growth driven only by enthusiasm.Creative people face similar choices. Whether writing, designing or developing software, completing one strong piece of work often provides a better platform than collecting unfinished ideas.The pace of modern communication encourages constant switching between priorities. Emails, messages and notifications compete for attention throughout the day, making uninterrupted work increasingly uncommon.Against that background, Page's words remain striking because they favour concentration over constant movement. The advice does not reject ambition. Instead, it asks whether ambition has been supported by consistent execution.Many organisations still rely on this principle when launching products. A reliable service with a clear purpose often earns trust more effectively than a broad collection of features that remain incomplete.
Article Summary: Larry Page is one of the co-founders of Google. He is known to emphasise the need to combine ambition and execution well. This focused approach builds confidence and a strong foundation for future endeavors. Rushing tasks can create future problems, while high standards require patience and revision.

Article Title: Kentucky family rejects $26 million offer to buy portion of their farm land for ‘poison’ AI data center, says ‘we know we’ve had it’
Article Text:
AI-generated image for representation purpose

Kentucky family says $26 million ‘doesn’t mean anything’

AI data centres lead to concerns over land, electricity and water

A Kentucky family has reportedly rejected an anonymous company's approach to turn a part of their farmland into an AI data centre. According to a report by WKRC (via Tom’s Hardware), land owner Ida Huddleston and her family were offered an extraordinary $26 million by the company which is presumed to be one of the major players in the industry. Despite the huge offer, the family refused to sell the land, which they have owned and farmed for generations. Huddleston said protecting farmland, food and natural resources was more important than the money.“They call us old stupid farmers, you know, but we’re not,” Huddleston said. “We know whenever our food is disappearing, our lands are disappearing, and we don’t have any water—and that poison. Well, we know we’ve had it.”The Huddleston family owns around 1,200 acres of farmland in Mason County in Northern Kentucky. According to the report, the AI company wanted to buy roughly half of the property to build a large data centre.The offer was significantly higher than typical land prices in the area. Farmland in Mason County reportedly sells for around $6,000 per acre, but the company offered the family $26 million – nearly 10X the local land value for the land it wanted to acquire.However, the family said its connection to the property goes beyond its financial value. Huddleston's daughter, Delsia Bare, said generations of their family have farmed the land and produced food for other families. She said their ancestors also grew wheat during the Great Depression and helped supply food when many Americans were struggling.“Stay and hold and feed a nation,” Bare told WKRC. “$26 million doesn’t mean anything.”The offer comes as technology companies are rapidly expanding AI infrastructure across the US. The growing use of generative AI requires companies to build large data centres packed with computing equipment.However, the expansion has also faced opposition in some communities because data centres can require large amounts of electricity and water. Residents in some areas have raised concerns about their possible impact on local power grids, water supplies and surrounding land.The company that approached the Huddleston family has not been identified. However, the report suggests that it has also approached other landowners in the surrounding area. Bare said some nearby property owners have agreed to sell their land. This means that despite the Huddleston family's refusal to accept the $26 million offer, the company could still potentially build its proposed AI data centre elsewhere in the area.
Article Summary: The Huddleston family owns around 1,200 acres of farmland in Mason County in Northern Kentucky. According to the report, the AI company wanted to buy roughly half of the property to build a large data centre. Farmland in the area reportedly sells for around $6,000 per acre, but the company offered the family $26 million.

Article Title: Etsy lays off 220 employees as CEO Kruti Patel Goyal restructures product and engineering teams; says its not linked to AI or cost-cutting
Article Text:
Etsy is reducing its workforce by approximately 220 employees, impacting its product and engineering divisions. This restructuring aims to simplify the company's organizational structure and support future growth initiatives. The online marketplace reported stronger-than-expected second-quarter revenue, exceeding analyst expectations. Etsy also raised its full-year forecast for gross merchandise sales, indicating positive momentum. Despite a slight decline in active buyers, the number of active sellers increased significantly.

"not a cost-cutting effort"

"You've heard me say that our first priority was to get the business growing again. Our ultimate goal, though, has always been to take Etsy to the next level of growth so we can fully deliver on our mission and our potential. We are now at the point where we need to make that shift - to build the team, culture, and organization that will make that possible,”

Etsy’s product and engineering teams most affected

"lean in during a period of strong momentum so that we can move faster and execute with even greater focus,"

"the organization we believe Etsy needs for the future."

Etsy raises outlook after stronger-than-expected quarter

Buyer numbers decline as Etsy focuses on core business

Etsy is laying off about 220 employees. The online marketplace said the cuts, affecting roughly 12% of its workforce, are part of a restructuring of its product and engineering teams under CEO Kruti Patel Goyal. The company said the decision is intended to simplify its organisational structure and support future growth, adding that the layoffs areand were not driven by artificial intelligence (AI). The workforce reduction was announced alongside Etsy's second-quarter earnings. In a memo to employees, Goyal said the company has reached a stage where it needs to reshape its organisation to support its next phase of growth.Goyal told CNBC.Etsy said most of the layoffs will impact its product and engineering teams. In its letter to shareholders, the company said the restructuring is designed to help itrather than reduce expenses.An Etsy spokesperson also said the job cuts were not driven by AI, addressing speculation that artificial intelligence was behind the workforce reduction. Goyal, who became CEO earlier this year, said the changes are aimed at buildingThe restructuring comes as Etsy reported second-quarter revenue of $668.3 million, exceeding analysts' expectations of $649.1 million, according to LSEG. Sales on Etsy's core marketplace increased 9.3% during the quarter.The company also raised its full-year forecast for gross merchandise sales (GMS), now expecting mid-single-digit growth, up from its earlier projection of low-single-digit growth. For the third quarter, Etsy expects GMS of $2.53 billion to $2.58 billion, above the FactSet consensus of $2.49 billion.Etsy continued to see a slight decline in active buyers, reporting 87 million buyers during the second quarter, down 0.4% year over year. However, the number of active sellers on the platform increased 5.9% to 5.7 million.The company has been focusing on strengthening its core marketplace by promoting handmade and unique products while removing mass-produced listings from resellers. In June, it launched its "Shop Other Jeffs" advertising campaign during Amazon's Prime Day event, highlighting products from "non-billionaire makers" named Jeff.Etsy also said it has improved search capabilities to deliver more personalised results and help shoppers discover products more quickly.
Article Summary: Etsy is reducing its workforce by approximately 220 employees, impacting its product and engineering divisions. This restructuring aims to simplify the company's organizational structure and support future growth initiatives. The workforce reduction was announced alongside Etsy's second-quarter earnings. Etsy also raised its full-year forecast for gross merchandise sales, indicating positive momentum.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Julie Sweet, ‘What's the greatest advice I give; Develop excellent communication skills’
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Julie Sweet

Quote of the day by Julie Sweet

What Julie Sweet's quote means

A message reflected in her work

A simple takeaway

Julie Sweet has spent her career moving from corporate law into the highest levels of global business leadership, eventually rising to CEO of Accenture, one of the world's largest consulting and professional services firms, overseeing hundreds of thousands of employees across more than 100 countries. Long before she reached that role, while leading Accenture's North America business, she was asked what the single best piece of career advice she gives is. Her answer wasn't about strategy, ambition, or technical mastery. It was about communication."What's the greatest advice I give? Develop excellent communication skills."An overlooked investment At first glance, the advice can sound almost too simple to be profound. Most professionals assume they already communicate reasonably well — after all, they speak, write emails, and sit through meetings every day. But Sweet's point is not about basic competence. It's about excellence, and about how rarely people treat communication as a skill worth deliberately investing in, the way they might invest in learning a new technical tool or industry certification.Why it stands out to leadership Sweet has pointed out that even junior employees who can clearly summarise a meeting, build a sharp presentation, or write a concise, well-organized email stand out immediately to leadership.In a world where technical skills are increasingly abundant and often interchangeable, the ability to translate complex ideas into something clear and persuasive becomes a genuine differentiator.The bridge between value and visibility There is also a broader truth about how organizations function embedded in the quote. Ideas, no matter how good, rarely succeed on their own merit alone — they succeed because someone was able to explain them well enough to get buy-in, funding, or collaboration. A brilliant analysis buried in a disorganized email may never be read closely enough to matter. A mediocre idea delivered with clarity and confidence can move an entire room. Communication, in Sweet's framing, is often the bridge between having value and being seen to have value.A skill she keeps practising What makes Sweet's advice particularly credible is that she treats it as an ongoing practice rather than a fixed trait some people are simply born with. She has spoken about spending dedicated time every year specifically to sharpen how she communicates — reviewing how she writes, how she presents, and how she delivers difficult messages.Scaling it to a global company That philosophy has scaled with her career. As Accenture's global CEO, when she needed to announce the biggest organizational restructuring in the company's history to a workforce of more than 770,000 people across 120 countries, she chose to deliver the message by video rather than through a written memo, reasoning that hearing the passion behind the change would land differently than reading about it on paper. She has also embedded communication and change-management training into every level of leadership development at Accenture, and has her own direct reports work with speech coaches to refine how they communicate. As she put it, to develop people, a leader has to be a great communicator — a principle she has carried from her earliest days in North America leadership all the way to the top of a global organisation.Sweet's advice endures because it applies at every career stage, from an entry-level employee trying to get noticed to a CEO trying to align a global workforce. Skills, credentials, and expertise open doors, but communication determines whether what's behind those doors is ever fully understood or acted upon. The next time a message, email, or presentation feels like an afterthought to "real" work, the relevant question is not "Did I get the information across?" It is "Did I get it across as clearly and persuasively as I could have?" Sweet is not suggesting communication is a soft, secondary skill. She is arguing that it is, quite often, the skill that decides whether every other skill gets noticed at all.
Article Summary: Julie Sweet is CEO of Accenture, one of the world's largest consulting and professional services firms. When asked what her best career advice was, she said: "Develop excellent communication skills" Sweet has embedded communication and change-management training into every level of leadership development at Accenture.

Article Title: Building Cloud resilience for India in an era of disruption
Article Text:
By

Bhawna Agarwal

, Senior Vice President and Managing Director,

HPE India

Recent global events have reinforced an important reality. Cloud infrastructure, while highly advanced, is not immune to disruption. Incidents impacting data center operations in parts of the Middle East earlier this year highlighted how dependent critical services have become on resilient digital infrastructure.For many years, organizations have viewed the cloud as inherently robust and always available. These developments offer a timely reminder that data centers are physical assets and part of a broader ecosystem that benefit from being designed with resilience at their core. As businesses and governments increasingly rely on digital platforms, ensuring continuity becomes essential.The opportunity and the imperativeIndia's data center market is projected to grow from $10 billion today to $22 billion by 2030. This growth is being driven by AI workloads, 5G rollout, and a policy environment that includes a tax holiday until 2047 for cloud providers, positioning India as a leading hub for digital infrastructure in Asia-Pacific.Scale also creates new and important considerations. As India absorbs more of the world's digital workloads, the infrastructure underlying that growth warrants being designed with resilience and continuity at its core.Data centers underpin banking, healthcare, logistics, and government services. Designing them for continuity, not just capacity, is one of the most consequential decisions in this phase of growth. Physical infrastructure is only half of the answer.India's challenge and responseThe other half is governance, and it is here that a second, equally consequential aspect comes into focus.Hosting data and controlling it are not the same thing. When cloud infrastructure is deployed without local governance controls, the encryption keys, operational authority, and legal jurisdiction over that data may sit outside the organization's reach. Sovereignty is not about where data sits. It is about who holds the keys, who governs the systems, and which laws apply when things go wrong. Even well-designed architecture may not deliver its full value if operational control does not sit with the entity running it. Resilience and sovereignty, in this sense, are not separate priorities. Together, they define a more complete approach to digital continuity.Recognising this does not mean retreating from global technology. It means ensuring that global technology aligns with India's regulatory, security, and operational requirements. Sovereignty is not weakened by foreign investment, but is strengthened when global players manufacture locally, innovate on Indian soil, and operate under Indian governance frameworks. Under Make in India and PLI schemes, enterprise-grade servers are now built in India at scale, with hundreds of patents filed from Indian R&D hubs across AI, cloud, and security. Tens of thousands of engineers in Indian cities are building systems deployed worldwide. The depth of this integration is significant. When global technology companies embed this deeply into India's industrial and innovation base and operate under Indian law, they become part of the country's sovereign capability.India's policymakers are actively building the framework to match this ambition. MeitY's updated Cloud Selection Framework now requires that sensitive government data, including systems supporting Aadhaar, UPI, tax, and passport services, be stored on sovereign infrastructure within the country. The national GI Cloud, MeghRaj, already supports over 300 government departments. Tamil Nadu has built its own cloud environment for 18 critical government applications, with a separate disaster recovery site. The RBI has required domestic storage of payment system data since 2018, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act tightens obligations further. Taken together, these initiatives reflect a governance framework that is maturing in step with the infrastructure being built. The direction is right. What must follow is the architecture to deliver on it.What resilience actually looks likeTranslating that policy intent into operational reality requires clarity on what resilient cloud architecture actually involves. Three capabilities define this in practice. The first is distributed architecture with no single point of failure. Workloads deployed across multiple locations, with automated failover that allows services to continue when any single region experiences disruption, provide the foundation of operational continuity. This is particularly relevant for India, where workloads span geographies and sectors with very different tolerances for downtime. Reducing dependency on any single provider or geography allows organizations to sustain services through the unexpected.The second is continuous data protection. Rather than relying on periodic snapshots, real-time replication captures every change as it occurs. This allows recovery to the most recent state within seconds of any disruption, substantially reducing data loss. Near-zero recovery objectives are achievable and represent a meaningful benchmark for organizations managing critical workloads.The third is sovereignty engineered into the design. A hybrid cloud model — private for regulated workloads and flexible where appropriate — with encryption keys, control planes, and data paths remaining within Indian jurisdiction, delivers both resilience and governance in a single architecture. Infrastructure designed to operate fully disconnected from external networks when required offers further assurance for sensitive workloads. With 73 percent of Indian enterprises reporting a shortage of qualified cybersecurity professionals, automated and intelligent systems that sustain this architecture across a hybrid estate are increasingly important to maintaining security at scale.Organizations that plan for these capabilities early are often better placed when continuity is tested. The broader point is not that every disruption can be avoided. It is that resilience works best when it is part of the design, rather than added later.Some will argue that existing backup protocols already go a long way. That is fair in many situations. The more instructive question is whether those protocols are sufficient for the scale and criticality of workloads India's infrastructure is now expected to carry. When infrastructure is disrupted at scale, organizations may need more than backups alone. They benefit from architectures that can recover quickly and keep core services available.For India, the conditions to build this kind of infrastructure have rarely been better aligned. The momentum is here. The policy direction is clear. The talent and technology to build genuinely resilient infrastructure exist within India's borders. The next phase of India’s digital journey will be defined not just by how fast India scales, but by how thoughtfully it designs for continuity, making resilience a core principle from the outset. Resilience is not a feature of the cloud; it is a choice made at the point of design.
Article Summary: India's data center market is projected to grow from $10 billion today to $22 billion by 2030. As India absorbs more of the world's digital workloads, the infrastructure underlying that growth warrants being designed with resilience and continuity at its core. Resilience and sovereignty, in this sense, are not separate priorities.
